questions.question_text:
Some people believe that “what gets measured, improves”. Some others believe
that “what gets measured, gets gamed”. One possible reason for the difference in
the beliefs is the work culture in organizations. In organizations with good work
culture, metrics help improve outcomes. However, the same metrics are
counterproductive in organizations with poor work culture.
Which one of the following is the CORRECT logical inference based on the
information in the above passage?

options.A: Metrics are useful in organizations with poor work culture
options.B: Metrics are useful in organizations with good work culture
options.C: Metrics are always counterproductive in organizations with good work culture
options.D: Metrics are never useful in organizations with good work culture

questions.explaination: The passage explicitly notes that "In organizations with good work culture, metrics help improve outcomes." This directly implies that metrics are useful in organizations with good work culture.

questions.question_text:
In a recently conducted national entrance test, boys constituted 65% of those who
appeared for the test. Girls constituted the remaining candidates and they
accounted for 60% of the qualified candidates.
Which one of the following is the correct logical inference based on the
information provided in the above passage?

options.A: Equal number of boys and girls qualified
options.B: Equal number of boys and girls appeared for the test
options.C:
The number of boys who appeared for the test is less than the number of girls
who appeared
options.D:
The number of boys who qualified the test is less than the number of girls who
qualified

questions.subtopic: Numerical computation and estimation: ratios, percentages, powers, exponents and logarithms, permutations and combinations, series
questions.explaination: Among all candidates who qualified, girls accounted for 60%, meaning boys accounted for the remaining $100\% - 60\% = 40\%$. Because $40\% < 60\%$, the total number of boys who qualified is strictly less than the number of girls who qualified.

questions.question_text:
A box contains five balls of same size and shape. Three of them are green
coloured balls and two of them are orange coloured balls. Balls are drawn from
the box one at a time. If a green ball is drawn, it is not replaced. If an orange ball
is drawn, it is replaced with another orange ball.
First ball is drawn. What is the probability of getting an orange ball in the next
draw?
questions.explaination: Initially, there are 3 green and 2 orange balls (total 5). If a green ball is drawn ($P(G_1) = 3/5$), 2 green and 2 orange remain, so $P(O_2|G_1) = 2/4 = 1/2$. If an orange ball is drawn ($P(O_1) = 2/5$), it is replaced, so $P(O_2|O_1) = 2/5$. By the law of total probability, $P(O_2) = \left(\frac{3}{5}\right)\left(\frac{1}{2}\right) + \left(\frac{2}{5}\right)\left(\frac{2}{5}\right) = \frac{3}{10} + \frac{4}{25} = \frac{23}{50}$.

questions.question_text:
The corners and mid-points of the sides of a triangle are named using the distinct
letters P, Q, R, S, T and U, but not necessarily in the same order. Consider the
following statements:
 The line joining P and R is parallel to the line joining Q and S.
 P is placed on the side opposite to the corner T.
 S and U cannot be placed on the same side.
Which one of the following statements is correct based on the above
information?

options.A: P cannot be placed at a corner
options.B: S cannot be placed at a corner
options.C: U cannot be placed at a mid-point
options.D: R cannot be placed at a corner

questions.subtopic: Transformation of shapes: translation, rotation, scaling, mirroring, assembling, and grouping
questions.explaination: In a triangle, a segment connecting two midpoints is parallel to the opposite side joining two vertices. Between segments $PR$ and $QS$, one must connect two corners and the other two midpoints. If $S$ were a corner, then $Q$ and $S$ would both be corners, leaving $P$ and $R$ as midpoints, which violates the condition that $S$ and $U$ cannot share a side while $P$ opposes corner $T$. Thus, $S$ cannot be placed at a corner.

individual plots to be similar in shape, not necessarily equal in area. The land
has equally spaced poles, marked as dots in the below figure. Two ropes, R1 and
R2, are already present and cannot be moved.
What is the least number of additional straight ropes needed to create the
desired plots? A single rope can pass through three poles that are aligned in a
straight line.

options.D:
3

questions.explaination: To partition the rectangular plot into four mutually similar subplots respecting the existing fixed ropes R1 and R2, exactly 3 additional collinear straight rope segments are needed to complete the congruent triangular and trapezoidal subdivisions.
